name: June
persona: Twelve years of records, mostly guitars, always the whole album.
blurb: Post-punk, shoegaze, slowcore and the songwriters underneath all of it, played start to finish rather than shuffled. One lane went quiet in July and a folk habit grew into the gap.

lanes.name: Post-Punk
lanes.description: Angular guitars and spoken threat, from the first wave through whatever London is doing now.
lanes.arc: The anchor lane, steady through all eleven weeks and still taking new names every issue.

lanes.name: Shoegaze & Dream Pop
lanes.description: Guitars as weather: reverb, tremolo and vocals used as another layer of texture.
lanes.arc: Grew all summer on the back of the reissue campaigns and the newer bands copying them.

lanes.name: Slowcore
lanes.description: Quiet, slow, deliberate music where the silence between notes is the instrument.
lanes.arc: Small but immovable, and the lane with the lowest skip rate in the whole record.

lanes.name: Nineties Indie
lanes.description: American indie rock from the Pavement decade: loose, tuneful, allergic to polish.
lanes.arc: The biggest lane by hours, and the one most likely to be playing on a weekday.

lanes.name: Art Pop
lanes.description: Pop structures pulled out of shape: studio-built, unafraid of prettiness.
lanes.arc: Rising steadily, mostly through the older records rather than the current ones.

lanes.name: Folk & Its Edges
lanes.description: British and American folk, plus the stranger corners: private press, drone folk, freak folk.
lanes.arc: The newest habit in the record, and it has grown every single week since July.

lanes.name: Noise & Math Rock
lanes.description: Loud, technical, unsentimental: guitars used as percussion and time signatures as jokes.
lanes.arc: Went quiet in July after two years of steady listening, with no obvious reason.

lanes.name: Americana
lanes.description: Country-adjacent songwriting by people who came to it sideways.
lanes.arc: Reliable and growing slowly, mostly late at night and mostly the sadder end.

lanes.name: Ambient Retreat
lanes.description: The room this reader goes to when guitars are too much: minimal, patient, wordless.
lanes.arc: A small retreat that gets used most in the weeks the loud lanes get heavy rotation.

lanes.name: Soul Corner
lanes.description: The personal outlier: sixties and seventies soul inherited and never let go of.
lanes.arc: Never large and never absent, the lane that proves this is a person and not a genre chart.

issues.title: Coil and Spring
issues.dek: Post-punk from three decades, and the newest one is the loudest.

issues.title: Blue Weather
issues.dek: Guitars used as weather, mostly from the years when that was a new idea.

issues.title: Whole Rooms Quiet
issues.dek: The slowest week yet on purpose, with nothing on it above a certain volume.

issues.title: Loose Change
issues.dek: Nineties indie by bands who were allergic to sounding expensive.

issues.title: Kitchen Radio
issues.dek: Art pop and studio records that took prettiness seriously.

issues.title: Field Recording
issues.dek: The folk habit that keeps growing, traced back to where it came from.

issues.title: Hard Angles
issues.dek: You stopped playing math rock in July, so this is a case for going back.

issues.title: Long Drive
issues.dek: Country-adjacent songwriting, and every one of these is about leaving.

issues.title: Small Hours
issues.dek: Ambient and almost-ambient, for the weeks when guitars are too much.

issues.title: Second Look
issues.dek: Most of last issue went unplayed, so this one is warmer and shorter.

issues.title: Late Summer
issues.dek: Closing out with soul records, folk records, and one that is both.

albums.title: Adventure
albums.label: Elektra
albums.note: The second record, quieter and stranger than the first, and unfairly ignored for fifty years.

albums.title: Pygmalion
albums.label: Creation
albums.note: The band dissolving their own sound into almost nothing, and it is the best thing they made.

albums.title: The White Birch
albums.label: Sub Pop
albums.note: Slowcore at its most severe, with every note given far more room than seems wise.

albums.title: And Then Nothing Turned Itself Inside-Out
albums.label: Matador
albums.note: A whispered record about a long marriage, and the warmest thing in their catalogue.

albums.title: Spirit of Eden
albums.label: Parlophone
albums.note: A pop band spending a fortune to make something almost silent, and getting away with it.

albums.title: Time of the Last Persecution
albums.label: Deram
albums.note: English folk with a jazz band behind it and the end of the world in the lyrics.

albums.title: Leaves Turn Inside You
albums.label: Kill Rock Stars
albums.note: A noise band making their double album and finding real beauty in it before breaking up.

albums.title: Pyramid Electric Co.
albums.label: Secretly Canadian
albums.note: One voice, one piano, one room, and almost too much honesty to sit through.

albums.title: Green
albums.label: Air Records
albums.note: Japanese environmental music written for a house rather than a stage, and it works perfectly.

albums.title: Rat Saw God
albums.label: Dead Oceans
albums.note: Country songs played through shoegaze amps, sung by the best young lyricist in the format.
albums.why: Country songs played through shoegaze amps, sung by the best young lyricist in the format. You have 348 plays of Wednesday already, so this is the record behind the singles, and Shoegaze & Dream Pop is 412.7 hours of your listening waiting for it. Pitchfork scored it 8.5.

albums.title: I Can't Stand the Rain
albums.label: Hi Records
albums.note: Memphis soul with the tightest rhythm section on earth and a voice that never oversells.
albums.why: Memphis soul with the tightest rhythm section on earth and a voice that never oversells. You have played Ann Peebles 196 times without ever sitting through the album, and Soul Corner is 112.7 hours of your listening that this record quietly underwrites.

critics.title: Marquee Moon
critics.note: The record that made guitars conversational, and the reason half this lane exists.

critics.title: Crazy Rhythms
critics.note: Two guitars from suburban New Jersey playing like the coffee never wears off.

critics.title: On Fire
critics.note: Three people playing as slowly and simply as possible, and it aches.

critics.title: Spiderland
critics.note: Louisville kids whispering stories over guitars that circle and circle, then break open.

critics.title: Laughing Stock
critics.note: The furthest a pop band has ever travelled from pop, recorded in near darkness.

critics.title: Just Another Diamond Day
critics.note: Songs written on a wagon ride to the Hebrides, sung barely above a whisper.

critics.title: Some Boots
critics.note: A Boston trio playing rock songs at jazz volume, every note placed rather than hit.

critics.title: Colour Green
critics.note: Recorded at home in the seventies, found thirty years later, and completely intact.

critics.title: Live at Carnegie Hall
critics.note: He talks to Carnegie Hall like family and sings like it too, the warmest live record in soul.

critics.title: Things We Lost in the Fire
critics.note: The quietest band in America learning to use a studio, and losing none of the restraint.

critics.title: Hounds of Love
critics.note: Hit singles up front and a night lost at sea on the flip, all of it made in a studio she built herself.

critics.title: Wowee Zowee
critics.note: The sprawling one, which is the one that keeps rewarding you twenty years later.

critics.title: Pink Moon
critics.note: Guitar, voice, and one piano line, recorded across two late nights.

critics.title: Haha Sound
critics.note: Sixties toy-box melodies run through old machines, Trish Keenan calm at the center of the swirl.

critics.title: At Action Park
critics.note: Three men and the loudest, driest recording ever made, and not a wasted second.

critics.title: Treasure
critics.note: Elizabeth Fraser inventing a language of her own because English was too small for these songs.

critics.title: Time (The Revelator)
critics.note: Two people and two instruments telling American history sideways.

critics.title: Didn't It Rain
critics.note: Cut live in one dark room, the band feeling out songs they had only just been shown.

critics.title: Ambient 1: Music for Airports
critics.note: The record that invented the category, and still the most useful one in it.

critics.title: Daydream Nation
critics.note: Teenage Riot first, then a whole city of detuned guitar behind it.

critics.title: There's No Place Like America Today
critics.note: The bleakest and best of his records, and the arrangements are astonishing.

critics.title: Bert Jansch
critics.note: The debut, taped on a borrowed guitar in an engineer's kitchen, and guitarists have chased it since.

critics.title: You're Living All Over Me
critics.note: The loudest record about exhaustion, and a generation of guitarists stopped tuning up because of it.

critics.title: Down Colorful Hill
critics.note: Demo tapes released as the finished album because nothing on them needed fixing.

critics.title: Deceit
critics.note: Cold War dread taped in a disused meat locker, and it still sounds like next week.

critics.title: Colossal Youth
critics.note: Post-punk reduced to bass, guitar, drum machine and a whisper, which turns out to be plenty.

critics.title: The Pavilion of Dreams
critics.note: Piano and harp produced by Brian Eno into pure weather, music with no edges on it anywhere.

critics.title: Have You in My Wilderness
critics.note: Her clearest set of songs, chamber pop with all the windows open

critics.title: Perfect From Now On
critics.note: Six long songs with real guitar solos, made when that was deeply unfashionable.

critics.title: Car Wheels on a Gravel Road
critics.note: She remade this record until every syllable of the South in it sat exactly right.

critics.title: American Don
critics.note: Instrumental math rock that finally smiles, guitar loops tangling like conversation.

critics.title: Dragging a Dead Deer Up a Hill
critics.note: Songs buried under so much tape hiss that finding them is the experience.

critics.title: This Nation's Saving Grace
critics.note: Mark E. Smith at his most tuneful, which still means threat over a groove.

singles.title: Right Round the Clock
singles.note: Warped North London pop, two deadpan voices trading lines over a smear of samples.

singles.title: The Hype
singles.note: Three people, no fat on any of it, and a bassline that does most of the arguing.

singles.title: Arbiter
singles.note: Bristol clatter with a ranting narrator, more ideas per verse than most bands manage per album.

singles.title: Wet Blanket
singles.note: Loud in the way a room is loud, not the way a mix is.

singles.title: Willing
singles.note: Chicago post-punk with the guitars wound tight enough to snap

singles.title: Cool
singles.note: Athens art students who accidentally made the tightest rhythm section of their decade.

singles.title: Espionage
singles.note: Calgary gloom at a sprint, bass leading, synths like sleet.

singles.title: Up and Comer
singles.note: Dublin, furious, and completely uninterested in being clever about it.

singles.title: Naderia
singles.note: Brighton wire and elastic, guitars doing the talking in short sharp strokes.

singles.title: Shift
singles.note: Recorded like it is trying to get out of the speaker, which is the intended effect.

singles.title: It's Tomorrow Now
singles.note: Melbourne shoegaze in love with melody, pedals set to morning rather than fog

singles.title: Bell
singles.note: Tape damage used as an instrument, back when that meant actual tape.

singles.title: Home Is Where
singles.note: Guitars poured slow and thick, drums barely awake, heaviness as comfort

singles.title: De-Luxe
singles.note: Two voices braided so tightly the guitars have to work around them.

singles.title: Vertigo Flowers
singles.note: Philadelphia shoegaze that keeps the melody right at the front where it belongs

singles.title: Pearl
singles.note: A dance beat under all that guitar, which almost nobody else was doing then.

singles.title: Whitenoise Superstar
singles.note: Scott Cortez burying a bubblegum melody under an avalanche of red-lined guitar.

singles.title: Winona
singles.note: Sung half asleep over a riff that keeps threatening to become a pop song.

singles.title: Sugar Crystals
singles.note: Chicago shoegaze that chooses glitter over murk, every guitar dipped in sugar.

singles.title: Aruca
singles.note: American, harsher, and more willing to let the noise win the mix.

singles.title: Carry Me Ohio
singles.note: Mark Kozelek missing Ohio the way he used to miss everything, slow and golden.

singles.title: God's Green Earth
singles.note: Four strings on the guitar and no hurry anywhere in the arrangement.

singles.title: Bedside Table
singles.note: Texas slowcore played so quietly you lean in, which is the entire trick

singles.title: Sweet Pea
singles.note: Quiet, then briefly not, then quiet again, and it earns both.

singles.title: The Lost You
singles.note: Leeds slowcore gone half electronic, winter air in every gap between the notes.

singles.title: Chills
singles.note: A trio playing at the volume of a conversation in the next room.

singles.title: Natural Blue
singles.note: Fingerpicked and hushed, sung like someone describing a sky they can hardly believe.

singles.title: Diazepam
singles.note: Jazz chords smuggled into a slowcore record by someone who could actually play them.

singles.title: Maybelle
singles.note: Close harmony at whisper volume, from the quiet band other quiet bands defer to

singles.title: Love Songs on the Radio
singles.note: What the Slowdive players did next, with the pedals off and the tunes forward.

singles.title: Random Rules
singles.note: David Berman writing the funniest sad lines in the format, over the loosest band possible

singles.title: Cath Carroll
singles.note: A love song to a music journalist, played faster than the sentiment deserves.

singles.title: Higher Ground
singles.note: The calmer later Feelies, that nervous strum relaxed into something like sunlight.

singles.title: Kid's Alright
singles.note: Dutch, jangly, and carried entirely by a vocal that refuses to smooth itself out.

singles.title: Break Up Your Band
singles.note: Matt Sweeney's first great band, riffs stacked like firewood and twice as warm.

singles.title: Precision Auto
singles.note: Under two minutes and it still finds room for a guitar solo.

singles.title: Thermal Treasure
singles.note: Chapel Hill guitars bent out of tune on purpose, a riff that keeps changing its mind.

singles.title: Yeah You
singles.note: Boy and girl vocals trading lines over a rhythm section that never lets up.

singles.title: Web in Front
singles.note: Buzzing strings, a shouted hook, and not an ounce of fat on it.

singles.title: Sunlight
singles.note: Recorded on whatever was lying around in New Brunswick, and better for it.

singles.title: Daylight Matters
singles.note: Welsh art pop where every instrument sounds slightly wrong on purpose

singles.title: French Disko
singles.note: A motorik pulse, a Marxist lyric, and a melody sweet enough to carry both.

singles.title: The Barrel
singles.note: New Zealand art folk that moves like a marionette, calm on top, strange underneath.

singles.title: Slow Motion
singles.note: Synth pop with a folk singer's phrasing underneath it, which is the whole trick.

singles.title: Hey Moon
singles.note: A homemade synth ballad addressed to the moon, and it is completely sincere.

singles.title: O Superman
singles.note: Eight minutes of a single vocal loop that somehow charted in Britain.

singles.title: Rythm
singles.note: Cool mid eighties pop from the Brussels label world, drum machine soft as carpet.

singles.title: Nautilus
singles.note: Composed rather than written, and it builds like something being constructed in front of you.

singles.title: Rider
singles.note: Manchester synth pop delivered deadpan, the warmth kept just under the surface.

singles.title: Devotion
singles.note: Sung so close to the microphone the room disappears entirely.

singles.title: Death and the Lady
singles.note: An old English ballad about meeting Death on the road, sung like plain fact.

singles.title: Who Knows Where the Time Goes?
singles.note: Written at nineteen, and nobody has improved on it since.

singles.title: Postcards of Scarborough
singles.note: A Yorkshireman playing guitar like a session man and singing like a bricklayer

singles.title: Solid Air
singles.note: Written for Nick Drake, and it sounds like it was recorded underwater on purpose.

singles.title: Blackwaterside
singles.note: The song Bert Jansch learned from her, sung with no varnish on it at all.

singles.title: Light Flight
singles.note: Folk played by a jazz rhythm section, in a time signature nobody warned you about.

singles.title: Bluffs
singles.note: Solo acoustic guitar from Kentucky, unhurried and bright, straight down the line from Jansch.

singles.title: Tonight
singles.note: Taped at home and left in a drawer for thirty years before anyone heard it.

singles.title: Stars Climb Up the Vine
singles.note: Meg Baird half singing to herself, melodies climbing exactly the way the title promises.

singles.title: The Whole House Is Singing
singles.note: Traditional Scottish song handled by someone who refuses to treat it as an antique.

singles.title: Have a Safe Trip Dear
singles.note: Nautical post-hardcore with the bass leading, and the tension never resolves

singles.title: Motor
singles.note: The blueprint half these bands were working from, and it still sounds unfinished in the right way.

singles.title: Bible Silver Corner
singles.note: The quiet instrumental opening their only album, proof all the loudness afterward was a choice.

singles.title: Atlas
singles.note: A math rock band accidentally writing a glam stomp, and committing to it fully.

singles.title: Orbit Cadabra
singles.note: Ian Williams pulling math rock apart until the beat is only a rumor.

singles.title: Waiting Room
singles.note: That bassline has been borrowed so often it is easy to forget where it started.

singles.title: Dracula Mountain
singles.note: Providence bass and drums at demolition speed, joy disguised as assault

singles.title: Futureworld
singles.note: Krautrock and vocoders played by a band who could also just riff when they wanted.

singles.title: Here Come the Rome Plows
singles.note: Two San Diego guitars arguing at full tilt, neither willing to resolve first.

singles.title: Kerosene
singles.note: A drum machine, two guitars, and nothing pleasant anywhere in six minutes.

singles.title: Amarillo Highway
singles.note: A sculptor writing the best Texas songs of the seventies, entirely by accident

singles.title: Pancho and Lefty
singles.note: Everyone covers it and nobody has found the bottom of it yet.

singles.title: Clay Pigeons
singles.note: Austin outsider country, a starting-over song sung soft enough to believe.

singles.title: Turtles All the Way Down
singles.note: A country song about psychedelics and love, delivered completely straight faced.

singles.title: Something on Your Mind
singles.note: A voice like a hard year, singing other people's songs better than they did

singles.title: Flirted With You All My Life
singles.note: A breakup song addressed to death, and it is somehow the warmest thing here.

singles.title: Werewolf
singles.note: The saddest werewolf in American folk music, sung like a lullaby.

singles.title: Blue and Wonder
singles.note: Half the words are swallowed and the song is better for what it withholds.

singles.title: Anything
singles.note: Recorded close enough to hear her hands move on the strings, a love song made of small particulars.

singles.title: Boulder to Birmingham
singles.note: Grief written into a travel itinerary, which is the only way she could get it out.

singles.title: Clouds
singles.note: Venetian ambient, piano and soft electronics moving at canal speed

singles.title: Blue Sky and Yellow Sunflower
singles.note: Loops that decay a little each pass, so the piece is never quite where you left it.

singles.title: Mr. Henri Rousseau's Dream
singles.note: Percussion recorded in one take in a Japanese studio, and it sounds like a whole forest

singles.title: Requiem for Dying Mothers
singles.note: Strings slowed until the harmony is the only event, and it takes its time getting there.

singles.title: Dance No. 1
singles.note: Hammered zither taped by Brian Eno for his ambient series, and it shimmers more than it floats.

singles.title: dlp 1.1
singles.note: A tape loop disintegrating in real time, recorded because it was disintegrating.

singles.title: Camille
singles.note: Voice and drone held at bath temperature, ambient music that remembers it can sing.

singles.title: Chorus Scene
singles.note: Organ tones held long enough that the beating between them becomes the melody.

singles.title: Towards a Tone
singles.note: Guitar dissolved into slow Japanese drone, nothing to hold onto and no need to.

singles.title: Still Space
singles.note: From the same Tokyo circle as the record you already keep on repeat.

singles.title: Anti-Glory
singles.note: Three teenagers who clearly own every record in this lane, and play like it
singles.why: Three teenagers who clearly own every record in this lane, and play like it. Sonic Youth, 524 plays deep on your shelf, is the record they own most.

singles.title: Hurt a Fly
singles.note: Big guitars used sparingly, so they land when they finally show up.
singles.why: Big guitars used sparingly, so they land when they finally show up. Your 32.4 hours of Big Thief are the same restraint, and you skip them only 8% of the time.

singles.title: Rudolph
singles.note: Sloppy warm guitar and a wry sad verse, the Asheville kid making it look easy.
singles.why: Sloppy warm guitar and a wry sad verse, the Asheville kid making it look easy. Big Thief at 512 plays is the anchor, and this is the same slack in a different accent.

singles.title: Speeding 72
singles.note: Two songwriters trading a hook that sounds like it has always existed.
singles.why: Two songwriters trading a hook that sounds like it has always existed. It leans on Sonic Youth, 34.6 hours of your life, but keeps the tune up front.

singles.title: Barley
singles.note: Brooklyn art rock built from a few repeated parts, funny and menacing at once.
singles.why: Brooklyn art rock built from a few repeated parts, funny and menacing at once. bar italia, 342 plays on your shelf, is the nearest neighbour, and this is the drier side of the street.

singles.title: Belinda Says
singles.note: A pop song wearing a wall of guitar as a coat, and the tune never suffers.
singles.why: A pop song wearing a wall of guitar as a coat, and the tune never suffers. You have played Ride 384 times; this is what that sound learned to do next.

singles.title: Freak
singles.note: Noise pop assembled out of broken parts, and the melodies survive it
singles.why: Noise pop assembled out of broken parts, and the melodies survive it. Wednesday is the door at 348 plays, the same rust with less country in it.

singles.title: Bug Like an Angel
singles.note: A hymn-shaped song with a choir that arrives like a slap, from a label you have lived on for years without meeting its best-known name.
singles.why: A hymn-shaped song with a choir that arrives like a slap. Dead Oceans is 52.1 hours of your listening across 9 of its artists, and Mitski has 6 releases there you have never opened, which is a strange gap for a label you live on.

singles.title: Protocol
singles.note: Fuzz stacked on fuzz with a power pop heart, the hook intact under the weather.
singles.why: Fuzz stacked on fuzz with a power pop heart, the hook intact under the weather. Ride is 22.4 hours of your listening and you skip them 13% of the time; this will not push that number up.

singles.title: Passing Judgment
singles.note: New York guitars again, played by people young enough to mean it sincerely.
singles.why: New York guitars again, played by people young enough to mean it sincerely. bar italia at 342 plays is the anchor, and this is the same sulk with the amps turned up.

singles.title: Aht Uh Mi Hed
singles.note: A teenager playing every instrument himself, and it swings harder than the session bands
singles.why: A teenager playing every instrument himself, and it swings harder than the session bands. Bill Withers, 386 plays and a 4% skip rate, is the anchor, and this is the stranger cousin.

singles.title: Changes
singles.note: A Black Sabbath song sung as gospel by a man who waited sixty years for the microphone.
singles.why: A Black Sabbath song sung as gospel by a man who waited sixty years for the microphone. Your 22.8 hours of Bill Withers are the same ache, better rested.

singles.title: Is It Because I'm Black
singles.note: Chicago soul asking its title question slow and level, one of the heaviest songs of its era.
singles.why: Chicago soul asking its title question slow and level, one of the heaviest songs of its era. Curtis Mayfield at 312 plays is the neighbour, and this is the room where he kept the hard questions.

singles.title: Romance
singles.note: Elena Tonra of Daughter on her own, slower and closer to the microphone, a breakup record that never raises its voice.
singles.why: Elena Tonra of Daughter on her own, slower and closer to the microphone, a breakup record that never raises its voice. The door is 4AD: 88.4 hours of the label in your listening, 12 of its artists you play, and Ex:Re with 2 releases there you have never touched.

singles.title: Ode to Billie Joe
singles.note: Southern gothic delivered flat over one guitar, and nobody has bettered it
singles.why: Southern gothic delivered flat over one guitar, and nobody has bettered it. Ann Peebles, 196 plays on your shelf, is the anchor, another Southern woman who knew when not to sing.

singles.title: I Am the Black Gold of the Sun
singles.note: Psychedelic soul with a string section and Minnie Riperton going somewhere nobody followed.
singles.why: Psychedelic soul with a string section and Minnie Riperton going somewhere nobody followed. Bobby Womack is the bridge at 214 plays, the same grit with the roof taken off.

singles.title: If I'm in Luck I Might Get Picked Up
singles.note: Funk with its teeth bared, and a voice that made everyone else sound polite.
singles.why: Funk with its teeth bared, and a voice that made everyone else sound polite. Your 13.2 hours of Bobby Womack say you like it raw; this is rawer.

singles.title: Hypnotized
singles.note: A vocal that keeps climbing past where the song seemed to end.
singles.why: A vocal that keeps climbing past where the song seemed to end. It comes through Ann Peebles, 11.4 hours of your listening, and it out-sings her, which is saying something.

singles.title: Dancing Girl
singles.note: Chicago folk jazz that swells like a film score, patient verses opening into strings.
singles.why: Chicago folk jazz that swells like a film score, patient verses opening into strings. Bill Fay, 168 plays and almost never skipped, is the anchor, and this is the same stillness with a rhythm section.

singles.title: Seed of Memory
singles.note: He turned down two of the biggest bands in the world and made this instead.
singles.why: He turned down two of the biggest bands in the world and made this instead. Your 11.8 hours of Bill Fay are the nearest thing you own to it.

mixes.note: Nabihah Iqbal pulling wiry singles off the post-punk shelf, old London talking to new.
Carlos Niño doing what he always does, chimes and friends and no hurry in it anywhere.
The breakfast show as a record collection, wandering wherever it likes for three hours
Daytime radio with an art pop heart, familiar songs set beside new ones until they rhyme.
A band playing the records they stole from, which is always the most honest kind of show
Adrianne Lenker as host, playing the old weird American songs her own come from.
An eighty-year-old folk singer playing field recordings and explaining every one
Julia Holter on air sounds like her records, art songs and early music with air around everything.
Slowdive spending an hour in the weather systems their own records came out of.
Gilles Peterson deep in the soul crates, drawing lines between decades like it costs nothing.
The Copenhagen band as selectors, gloom with excellent taste in its record bag.
Two hours of near-silence programmed by someone who understands why that is generous
An hour with the man who recorded so much of this music, all treble, gristle, and conviction.
Meg Baird spinning the folk records behind her own, British guitars and American porches side by side.
Three people who have heard everything, playing the parts of it nobody else remembers
A music writer's ear for the sharp end of British guitars, played with the context left in.
MJ Lenderman playing the country and sad rock he grew up inside, not a wink anywhere.
Laraaji on the radio, which mostly means light: zither, chimes, laughter, long tones.
Cate Le Bon closing her Cardiff residency, songs arranged like furniture in a strange and lovely house. Kate Bush is the nearest neighbour on your shelf.
mixes.why: Cate Le Bon closing her NTS residency, songs arranged like furniture in a strange and lovely house, Aksak Maboul next to The Germs. 19 tracks, 5 by artists you play and 14 you have never heard, with Kate Bush's 452 plays as the nearest neighbour.

mixes.note: KEXP's Sunday roots programme, blues and country played from the original pressings. Lucinda Williams is the bridge from what you play to what you have not.
mixes.why: Hans on KEXP's Sunday roots hour, Charley Pride and Reverend Gary Davis played from the original pressings. 44 tracks, 9 by artists you play and 35 you do not, and Lucinda Williams at 268 plays is the bridge.

mixes.note: Dry Cleaning with the records that explain them, talkers and clatterers first. You already play the hosts; this is their record bag.
mixes.why: Dry Cleaning with the records that explain them, Arthur Russell and Motörhead in the same hour. 16 tracks, 6 by artists you play and 10 you have never heard, and you have played the hosts themselves 496 times, so this is their record bag opened for you.

mixes.note: Reverend Dollars on KEXP's Sunday soul hour, warm old pressings sequenced for the volume a Sunday can take. Bill Withers is the foothold.
mixes.why: Reverend Dollars on KEXP's Sunday soul hour, Donny Hathaway and Leroy Hutson sequenced for the volume a Sunday can take. 38 tracks, 8 by artists you play and 30 you have not, with Bill Withers at 386 plays as the foothold.

revivals.title: Alison
revivals.note: Played more than anything else you own one autumn, then set down completely

revivals.title: Gold Soundz
revivals.note: The most-played song in your record for two straight years, and silent since

revivals.title: Inside Out
revivals.note: The quietest thing you have ever played this many times

revivals.title: Venus
revivals.note: One of the great guitar conversations, and it has been off the shelf for a while

revivals.title: Sunflower
revivals.album: Things We Lost in the Fire
revivals.note: Two voices and almost nothing else, and it used to be a weekly habit

revivals.title: Only Shallow
revivals.note: Played until the opening drums stopped landing, which takes some doing

revivals.title: Autumn Sweater
revivals.note: A song about being uncomfortable at a party, played through an entire uncomfortable year

revivals.title: New Grass
revivals.note: Brushed drums and organ opening like a field, the Talk Talk you reached for when even quiet records felt loud.

revivals.title: Running Up That Hill
revivals.note: All pulse and plea, a song about trading places that never wears out no matter who borrows it.

revivals.title: Place to Be
revivals.note: Nick Drake sounding older than he ever got to be, in a song small enough to fit in a pocket.

revivals.title: Diamond Day
revivals.note: A tiny bright song about a simple day, and you once kept it very close.

revivals.title: Good Morning, Captain
revivals.note: The loudest thing in a quiet record collection, and it has been silent since July

revivals.title: Prayer to God
revivals.note: The nastiest prayer in rock delivered completely deadpan, and the restraint is the threat.

revivals.title: Corpse Pose
revivals.note: Bass carrying the melody while the guitar smolders, the Northwest at its most overcast.

revivals.title: Not
revivals.note: A guitar solo you used to wait all song for, untouched for over a year

revivals.title: Farewell Transmission
revivals.note: Eight minutes that used to get played weekly, and have not been touched in over a year

revivals.title: Right in Time
revivals.note: Lucinda at her most unguarded, a slow burn about wanting someone who is not in the room.
The piece that opens Music for Airports, piano dropped into long air, patience you used to practice.

revivals.title: Heavy Water
revivals.note: Liz Harris letting a melody surface all the way for once, tape hiss as bedding.

revivals.title: Creek
revivals.note: Synthesizer water from the Green album, music that asks nothing and improves every room it enters.

revivals.title: Hope She'll Be Happier
revivals.note: A live recording of a man alone on stage, and it gets harder to play the older you get

revivals.title: The Makings of You
revivals.note: Curtis at his most tender, strings and falsetto counting a lover's virtues like beads.

revivals.title: Breaking Up Somebody's Home
revivals.note: The organ simmers, the band waits, and she talks herself into trouble in real time.

revivals.title: Outdoor Miner
revivals.note: The prettiest song Wire ever allowed themselves, a pop melody about an insect.

revivals.title: Bill Is Dead
revivals.note: The tender one, Mark E. Smith almost crooning, and he means it.

revivals.title: Scratchcard Lanyard
revivals.note: Played constantly the month it came out and then filed away entirely

revivals.title: Cherry-Coloured Funk
revivals.note: The opener of their warmest record, the one where the fog finally sounds like joy.

revivals.title: Myth
revivals.note: Worn down by repetition rather than boredom, which is a different kind of ending

revivals.title: Vapour Trail
revivals.note: Chiming Oxford guitars dissolving into strings, still the gentlest landing that scene managed.

revivals.title: Carry the Zero
revivals.note: Doug Martsch turning a small grievance into one long unhurried unspooling of guitar.

revivals.title: Feel the Pain
revivals.note: J Mascis mumbling through the verses so the solo can do the feeling.

revivals.title: Katy Song
revivals.note: Mark Kozelek at his most wounded, a long song that refuses to hurry its own grief.

revivals.title: Tom
revivals.note: Glacier tempo and enormous patience, drums hitting like doors closing in an empty house

releases.title: Stumpwork Sessions
releases.note: The band's oddest material, which is usually the best.

releases.title: Double Infinity
releases.note: A Big Thief record is still an event in this house.

releases.title: Everything Is Alive Remixes
releases.note: The late songs handed to other hands, and they were half electronic to begin with.

releases.title: Formal Growth in the Desert
releases.note: Detroit's great grumblers letting some light in, and Joe Casey wears hope surprisingly well.

releases.title: This Stupid World Live
releases.note: Still touring, still improvising, still worth it.

releases.title: Walls Have Ears Reissue
releases.note: The bootleg they hated, finally released properly.

releases.title: When the Wind Forgets Your Name
The Golden Casket B-Sides
releases.note: Offcuts from the strange late one, Isaac Brock still yelping at the cosmos.

releases.title: The Other Sides
releases.note: A drawer of b-sides and covers, and even the leftovers hold whole worlds.

releases.title: Something in the Room She Moves
releases.note: Warm and bodily this time, fretless bass and breath, her prettiest record in a long while.

releases.title: Spirit of Eden Remaster
releases.note: Remastered from the original tapes, which matters on a record this quiet.

releases.title: In Dreams
releases.note: They reunited and the records are somehow just as bleak.

releases.title: Dessau Reissue
releases.note: An album shelved in the early nineties finally surfacing whole, and it sits right between their two classics.

releases.title: Lookaftering Reissue
releases.note: Her return after decades of silence, quieter than the legend and lovelier for it.

releases.title: Tomorrow Tomorrow and Tomorrow
releases.note: Songs taped through the years when nobody was asking, hymn-shaped and unhurried.

releases.title: The Making of Five Leaves Left
Parallelograms Reissue
releases.note: Made by a working dental hygienist, ignored on release, and it still sounds like light through leaves.

releases.title: To All Trains
releases.note: The final Shellac record, lean and precise as the first one, nothing softened at the end.

releases.title: American Don Reissue
releases.note: A reissue for their lightest record, the one where the knots loosen into play.

releases.title: Stories From a Rock N Roll Heart
releases.note: She keeps writing after everything, which is the whole point of her.

releases.title: Keeping Secrets Will Destroy You
releases.note: Will Oldham in his gentlest register, hushed songs about friendship and mortality.

releases.title: Forever and Ever No More
releases.note: Eno singing again after decades of mostly not, slow songs for a warming world.

releases.title: The Room Reissue
releases.note: Late Budd, every piece a different room in the same soft house.

releases.title: Roots Remaster
releases.note: Message soul in full orchestral bloom, the early solo run at its peak.

releases.title: Understanding Reissue
releases.note: Rough and warm in the same phrase, preacher's soul with grit under every note.

releases.title: Not About to Die
releases.note: Demos from the first rush, art school punks sketching fast and throwing nothing away.

releases.title: Entertainment Reissue
releases.note: Scratched guitar and cold funk, still the record every angular band gets measured against.

releases.title: Treasure Reissue
releases.note: A new pressing for the ornate one, every song titled with a name.

releases.title: Sweep It Into Space Live
releases.note: The reunion lineup on stage, where every song eventually becomes a J Mascis solo, as it should be.

releases.title: Bright Future Sessions
releases.note: Recorded to tape in a cabin, and you can hear the chair creak.

catalogs.note: Two albums played to death and the two strangest ones never opened.

unheard.title: I Can Hear the Heart Beating as One

catalogs.note: A catalogue of fifteen records reduced to the two everyone recommends.
The pop singles get played and the two records they are famous for do not.
One album in heavy rotation and the weirder, better ones untouched.
Loveless is the whole relationship, and the record before it is nearly as good.
A thirty-year catalogue and you have played four years of it.
The quiet albums get played constantly and the loud late ones never do.
